comments.text:
People often dismiss AI by saying: “It’s not really reasoning — it just builds or uses tools to solve problems.”

But let’s pause for a second. For decades, we’ve recognized tool use as a hallmark of intelligence in animals. When chimps strip branches to fish termites, or when crows bend wires to grab food, we don’t say, “That’s cheating.” We say, “Wow, that’s smart.”

Humans are the ultimate example. Our entire civilization is built on tools. We invented math, telescopes, programming languages, and airplanes — not because we could solve everything “in our heads,” but because building tools is exactly what intelligence does.

So why should AI be judged differently? If a model recognizes its own limits and creates or applies external tools to overcome them, that’s not a flaw — that’s a feature. It’s displaying the same adaptive behavior we associate with every other definition of intelligence.

The question isn’t whether AI thinks like us. The real question is: Are we holding AI to a different standard than we do ourselves?

It’s pretty homo-centric of us to presume that our definition (whatever that might be) of “reasoning” matters. What’s the goal of the reasoning? What inputs are there and what outputs are expected? If the machine (a person or an LLM/AI/whatever) takes the inputs and produces the expected (as opposed to correct) output, then how they got there is somewhat immaterial.

Also, we keep looking for this point at which these things we have created are “as smart as a human”. We don’t even know how smart a human is, nor how to measure “smartness”. IQ tests are known to be flawed. We have battery after battery of tests that AIs are expected to pass, and they beat humans so often in those tests that we’ve become inured to the news of yet another model beating humans, changing the goalposts as we go to ensure that we’re comfortable in the idea that we’re not being overtaken.

In a Capitalist society, the vast majority of humans are needed to provide labor functions. We have been being replaced in that function for almost two hundred years — even longer depending on how you track it. Yet we keep creating more humans, further diluting the shrinking pool because of some misguided idea of our own importance. Capitalists don’t care if a machine is smarter than a human, they care that a machine, which doesn’t require sick days, vacations, benefits, raises, or anything beyond acquisition and maintenance costs, can do a task reliably. If a machine can be demonstrated that does a necessary task reliably, it will be used to replace a human every time.

AGI? Someday. But it won’t matter by then.

comments.text:
Let me break it down. If we define AGI as the ability to mimic or outperform humans in academic-style testing, then most LLMs today could be considered AGI, because they can already achieve that. And if we keep creating more difficult exams and benchmarks, and LLMs continue to surpass them, then by that definition AGI would be achieved.

But here’s the problem: human intelligence is not about scoring 100% in statistics, calculus, or geometry. A straight-A student doesn’t necessarily succeed in the real world just because they aced their exams. Similarly, LLMs excel at pattern recognition and possess predictive abilities unlike anything we’ve seen before—but that alone doesn’t equate to true intelligence.

That being said, this capability is already remarkable. The potential applications are not just numerous, but nearly infinite. Still, claiming that LLMs will become more intelligent than humans is questionable. Yes, LLMs today can perform at a PhD level on many benchmarks—but have they produced any truly novel scientific discoveries? (AlphaGo, for example, is not an LLM; its achievements stem from advanced pattern recognition.)

So where are the breakthroughs? LLMs operate at a scale far beyond humans, so in theory, they should already be producing them—but they aren’t.
